Greater kudu neonates, specifically female calves, enter the world at a surprisingly modest mass given the species' substantial adult dimensions; field records from savanna populations indicate that a newborn female weighs approximately 15,000 grams [Wwb = approximately 15,000 grams] at parturition. This altricial-like birth weight, however, belies a remarkably rapid growth trajectory during the first weeks of life, when the calf remains concealed in dense thicket vegetation under the watchful care of its dam. The suckling juvenile depends entirely on milk during this initial phase, gradually transitioning to browse as it matures. The pronounced difference between neonatal mass and the ultimate body size achieved by adults underscores a life-history strategy in which early investment in a large, well-developed calf at birth may reduce predation vulnerability. Comparative data from related tragelaphine antelopes suggest that this birth weight is consistent with a pattern of extended gestation and a relatively precocial neonatal state, allowing the calf to follow its mother within days of delivery. Observations of marked individuals in protected reserves confirm that these birth masses are surprisingly consistent across various habitat types, from miombo woodlands to arid thornveld.

At the core thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this endothermic ungulate, 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C], female kudu reach the onset of gonadal activity at an age of approximately 488 days since birth [tp = approximately 488 days since birth], reflecting a relatively prolonged juvenile phase compared to smaller bovids. Males, in contrast, require a substantially longer developmental interval before attaining sexual maturity, with puberty recorded at roughly 732 days since birth [tp = roughly 732 days since birth] under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in maturation timelines is closely linked to the species' polygynous mating system, where males must achieve a larger body size and social standing before successfully competing for access to receptive females. During the sub-adult period, young bulls often form bachelor groups while continuing to grow, delaying any serious reproductive attempts until several years after the physiological onset of puberty. The somatic growth trajectory during this phase is steep, with males investing heavily in skeletal elongation and the development of the characteristic spiraled horns that are crucial for dominance displays. Females, by contrast, channel resources into earlier reproductive readiness, allowing them to begin breeding as soon as they reach a viable body condition.

Gestation in Greater kudu, when assessed at a maternal core body temperature of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C], lasts for approximately 244 days [tg = approximately 244 days] before parturition occurs, a duration typical of large-bodied antelopes inhabiting seasonal environments. This extended period of in utero development ensures that the foetus reaches an advanced state of neurological and locomotory maturation, enabling the calf to rise and follow the dam within hours of delivery. The timing of parturition is closely synchronized with the onset of the wet season across much of the species' range, ensuring that lactating females have access to abundant, high-quality forage to meet the elevated energetic demands of milk production. Following birth, the nursing offspring remains heavily dependent on maternal provisioning for the first half-year of life. Data collected from radio-collared individuals in Kruger National Park indicate that weaning, or the cessation of suckling, occurs at approximately 183 days [tx = approximately 183 days] after the birth event, when the juvenile has developed sufficient rumen function to subsist entirely on brow at a temperature of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C]se. This nutritional emancipation marks a critical transition in the life cycle, as the young kudu must then navigate the dual challenges of predator avoidance and food acquisition without maternal support.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Greater kudu in natural settings, measured under typical thermoregulatory conditions of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C], reaches approximately 8,578 days [am = approximately 8,578 days], representing a longevity that places the species among the longer-lived of the tragelaphine antelopes. This impressive lifespan is accompanied by a correspondingly slow reproductive pace, with females producing at most a single calf per parturition [N_R_i = single calf per parturition] and often skipping years entirely under poor environmental conditions. The maximum annual reproductive output achieved by a female kudu is one calf per year, reflecting the high maternal investment required to produce a large, well-developed neonate capable of surviving predation pressure. Field studies in the Serengeti ecosystem have confirmed that even under optimal foraging conditions, twin births are exceptionally rare in this species and are almost never recorded. This low fecundity is offset by a high survival rate of the juvenile once it reaches weaning age, particularly when mothers successfully conceal their calves during the vulnerable neonatal period. Comparisons with sympatric antelope species such as impala, which produce multiple offspring annually, highlight the markedly slower life-history pace of the kudu.

Adult body mass in Greater kudu exhibits one of the most pronounced examples of sexual size dimorphism among African bovids, a pattern that directly influences both social behavior and reproductive strategy. The dimorphism is driven by males reaching an ultimate wet weight of 270,000 grams [Wwi = 270,000 grams], nearly 30 percent heavier than the 210,000 gram [Wwi = 210,000 gram] asymptotic mass of females, a disparity intimately linked to intrasexual competition for mating opportunities. This dimorphism in adult body mass is accompanied by a parallel divergence in growth trajectories; males continue somatic development for several years beyond female maturation, investing in the large body frame and massive horn structure necessary for successful dominance contests. The ecological implications of this size difference are substantial, with males capable of reaching higher browse layers and thus accessing forage unavailable to the smaller females during dry season bottlenecks. Predation risk also scales with body size, as the larger adult males are less vulnerable to ambush predators like leopards but may face greater energetic costs during food scarcity. The pronounced sexual dimorphism observed in this species serves as a textbook example of how life-history trade-offs shape morphology across the sexes in polygynous ungulates.
